content:
Apple is strongly opposing the Department of Justice's attempt to overturn a court ruling that allowed the company to request documents from more than a dozen federal agencies. Here are the details.

A little background

A few weeks ago, Apple won the right to request documents from 14 U.S. agencies as part of its defence against the antitrust case the Department of Justice filed against the company in March 2024.

These include the following agencies and departments:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Department of Commerce
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Department of Defense
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • Department of State

Apple's argument is that if it can prove the federal government selected its products based on their privacy features, that evidence could support its claim that the practices challenged by the DOJ have legitimate reasons and are not anticompetitive behaviour.

After Apple won this dispute, the DOJ immediately filed a motion asking retired federal judge Jose Linares, who is serving as a special master of evidence in the case, to reconsider his decision.

In complex cases involving extensive discovery, courts sometimes appoint a special master to resolve narrower disputes and ease the workload of the presiding judge. A special master can be a retired judge, a practising attorney, or another expert with relevant experience.

In its motion, the DOJ asked the court to overturn Apple's discovery win, arguing that Judge Linares applied the wrong legal standard by treating the agencies as parties to the case rather than non-parties entitled to greater discovery protections.

The DOJ also claimed Apple's demands would impose an undue burden on the agencies involved, citing 13 newly submitted declarations as support, and argued that because federal agencies are not 'ordinary consumers', the relevance of the requested documents is limited.

"This motion has no merit at any level"

Apple's response to the DOJ's motion is now public, and the company unequivocally rebuts each of the DOJ's arguments for overturning the ruling point by point.

Citing multiple precedents, Apple argued that "the Special Master correctly applied the legal standard for party discovery against federal agencies," and systematically dismantled the DOJ's arguments on undue burden and relevance.

Apple stated in its conclusion:

Per the schedule Judge Linares set on August 4, no further briefing will be accepted, and it is now up to him to decide whether to uphold the original discovery order or grant the DOJ's request for reconsideration.
